title: How to squat to maximize muscle growth and minimize injury risks
summary: NH gives squat pointers rarely covered elsewhere: initiate with knee flexion rather than a hip hinge to avoid turning the squat into a good morning, narrow the grip progressively to keep the upper back packed, low bar for tall lifters, a four-step walkout, finishing reps before re-racking, a controlled positive, and a lying glute-flex trick to find foot angle.
claims: For someone adapted to it, the squat is the best way to grow the legs and should be the main knee-flexion pattern, with variations built around it
The squat is demanding on the lower back; many people get more lower back pain from squats than deadlifts
The squat is a knee flexion, not a hip hinge: initiate by breaking at the knees and let the posterior chain engage naturally
Hip hinging first then squatting turns the lift into a good morning, overloads the lower back and reduces quad involvement
Breaking at the knees first allows a more vertical torso and less lower back involvement
If you good morning the same way you squat, or stiff-leg deadlift like you deadlift, your technique is wrong
Behind-the-neck presses are not dangerous per se; the load makes them dangerous
Start squat warm-ups with a wider grip and progressively narrow it until you can pack the upper back
Never relax the upper back during the squat; losing thoracic extension leads to a rounded spine in the hole
Elbows appearing to move back is just the torso leaning forward; that is fine as long as the upper back stays packed
Elbows moving and pushing the bar causes forward lean; poor shoulder mobility can cause this too
Try both high bar and low bar; tall men with long legs are usually better off with low bar because high bar involves too much lower back
High bar technically recruits more quads, but for tall men low bar keeps a static torso angle so the legs do more
Ass-to-grass is not an objective standard; depth depends on leverages, and a tall man's partial travels more distance than a short man's full squat
Beginners need not squat ass to grass without the mobility; advanced lifters can use both full range and parallel partials
Butt wink: cut the range of motion before the butt tucks under, and avoid pushing the butt back before descending
Unrack from directly under the bar with the upper back packed, effectively a partial squat, so the next set is not a hassle
Walk out in about four steps, widening the stance with each step to land in your final stance without shuffling
Never step forward toward the rack before locking out the rep; finish the rep and lock the knees before re-racking
He likes slow negatives; the positive should be explosive but controlled, never so violent the bar comes off the back
The squat is a safe lift, though not as safe as the deadlift
Find your stance width by experimenting; very narrow destroys his knees
Knees past toes is fine, but excessive forward travel overuses the quads and underuses glutes and hamstrings
Lie down, lift the legs and flex the glutes: the resulting foot rotation approximates your ideal squat foot angle and builds glute mind-muscle connection
exercises: break at knees first, pack upper back, narrow grip, bar on traps
more horizontal torso, push the bar
distinct from squat; squatting like it is wrong
legs in the air, flex glutes, watch feet rotate
finds squat foot angle; glute mind-muscle connection
